title: The Astronomer's Daughter
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: There were seventeen boxes in her father's office when she opened it. Her father had been dead six weeks. He had, in the last years of his life, packed the whole of his professional work into these boxes, labeled by year in his own careful handwriting. The seventh box was different. The notebooks in the seventh box were black.

chapters.title: The Boxes
chapters.body:
There were seventeen boxes in her father's office when she opened it.

Her father had been dead six weeks. He had been dying, more or less, for eleven years, of the slow neurological condition that had, over that time, taken from him first his ability to work at his own instruments, then his ability to read, then his ability to speak with any fluency, and finally, in the last four months, his ability to eat without help. Priya Ramesh had spent the last three years traveling to see him — from Cambridge to Bangalore twice a year, then three times a year, then, in the last year, once every two months — and had been at his bedside for the last night, and had, on the small morning after, understood that a very long thing had finally ended.

She had stayed in Bangalore for the funeral, and for the two weeks after during which her mother had needed her at close range, and had then, at her mother's insistence, gone back to Cambridge to resume her own life. She was thirty-three. She was a postdoctoral researcher in observational cosmology at the Institute of Astronomy, and she had, she was reminded gently by her supervisor via email, a paper due in six weeks and a telescope allocation on the William Herschel in ten.

She had returned to Cambridge. She had resumed her work. She had, over the course of the next month, done the small necessary things that had to be done after a father died — the emails to his old students, the note in the departmental newsletter, the small acknowledgments accepted at the mid-morning tea. She had, by the end of that month, believed herself to be functional.

Her mother had called on a Thursday evening.

Her mother had said: *the office is still full of his things. I cannot go in there. Will you come and sort them.*

Priya had said: *of course.*

She had flown back the following week.

The office was on the ground floor of the small house in Malleshwaram where she had grown up. It was the room her father had used for the whole of his professional life, from the year he had bought the house at thirty-one until the year, eleven years ago, when the disease had first prevented him from going into it. He had, in his working years, spent most of every evening in it. He had spent Sunday mornings in it. Priya had, as a child, been permitted to come in only when he called her, and had come in when he called her, and had left when he told her to leave. It was, in the specific way of Indian middle-class houses of the sort her father had come to own, his room.

She had opened the door.

The room smelled of old paper and dust and the faint chemical sweetness of the sandalwood soap her mother had put in the drawers years ago and never removed. The desk was where it had always been. The bookshelves along the north wall were where they had always been. The small round table where he had done his calculations was where it had always been.

Piled around the room, on every horizontal surface, were the boxes.

Priya had, at first, thought they were her mother's. Her mother had, in the last year, been slowly moving her father's things out of the room, because she had wanted to reclaim it as a sitting room and had not, in the event, been able to bring herself to enter it after he had died. Priya had, on that first afternoon, assumed the boxes were her mother's collections of his things.

She had opened one.

She had stood in the middle of the office for a long time.

The boxes were her father's own. He had, in the last years of his ability to move, moved everything he had ever produced — every notebook, every draft, every letter, every calculation — into the office, and had, systematically, over what must have been many months, packed it all into these seventeen boxes, labeled by year in his own careful handwriting.

The label on the top of the first box read: *1971–1978.*

The label on the second read: *1979–1984.*

She had opened the third. *1985–1988.* She had opened the fourth. *1989–1993.*

She had sat down on the small round table.

She had thought, for a moment, that she should not do this alone. That she should get her mother. That she should get her brother. That she should get one of her father's old colleagues, some professor of forty years' acquaintance, to help her sort through it, because forty years of a working astronomer's notebooks was not a job for a daughter on a Wednesday afternoon.

She had understood, however, sitting on the small round table, that she was going to do it alone. That her father had, in packing the boxes himself, made a choice about who would open them. That her mother could not enter the office, and that her brother had, since childhood, avoided their father's things with a specific carefulness that Priya had never entirely understood, and that of the three of them she was, as she had always been in matters concerning her father's work, the one who would look.

She had opened the fifth box.

She had started reading.

—

The early boxes were unremarkable.

They were, so far as she could tell, the working notebooks of a competent Indian astronomer of the seventies and eighties, producing regular papers on stellar photometry, on the variable stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, on the first careful spectroscopic work coming out of the recently upgraded Kavalur observatory. There were letters — carbon copies, in her father's careful English — to colleagues in Cambridge and Berkeley and Sydney. There were referee reports. There were drafts of talks. There was, in one file, the whole of the correspondence surrounding her father's decision, at thirty-eight, not to accept an appointment at Berkeley that had, she had never known before, been formally offered him.

She had read this file with the particular quiet feeling of learning something one's father had decided not to say.

She had, by the end of the third day, finished the first six boxes. She had made three small piles. Papers to be preserved, for the departmental archive. Personal correspondence to be preserved for the family. Old drafts and calculations to be recycled. The piles were about equal.

She had come, on the fourth day, to box seven.

Box seven was labeled *1998–2002.*

Priya had been born in 1993. In 1998 she had been five. In 2002 she had been nine. She had, in that period, been present in her father's life as a small girl who was sometimes called into the office to help with a small task — to hand him a book from the shelf, to be told a small thing about a picture on the wall, to be shown a slide of the moon at the eyepiece of the small refractor he kept on the balcony. She had, that period, been the child who thought her father was the most important person in the world.

She had opened box seven.

She had, immediately, seen that box seven was different.

—

The notebooks in box seven were of a different color.

Her father's ordinary working notebooks had, throughout the earlier boxes, been the standard cloth-bound blue ledgers used at Bangalore observatories in that period. There had been dozens of them. They had been consistent.

The notebooks in box seven were black.

They were smaller. They were of a different make. They were, so far as she could tell from a first inspection, a specific brand of leather-bound field notebook that a particular firm in London had produced, in small quantities, in the nineties. Her father had, at some point in the late nineties, begun a separate set of notebooks in a different color, kept in a different box.

She had opened the first one.

It was, at first, unremarkable. Astronomical observations. Coordinates. Dates. Small notes on seeing conditions. But the coordinates — she saw within a few pages — were not the coordinates of any of the standard survey fields she knew her father had been working on in that period. They were not the coordinates of the fields listed in his published papers. They were coordinates in Cepheus, and in Cassiopeia, and in a small region on the boundary between Perseus and Andromeda. They were, as far as she could tell at a first glance, coordinates of empty sky.

She had turned the pages.

The observations continued. Night after night. Nineteen ninety-eight into nineteen ninety-nine into two thousand. Coordinates. Dates. Small careful measurements. On some nights her father had written a single word beside the entry — *still,* or *weaker,* or, once, *closer.*

She had turned back to the coordinates.

She had opened a star atlas from her father's bookshelf — the old Norton's, the one he had given her at nine — and had begun to look up the coordinates.

She had found, at each coordinate, nothing.

Not stars. Not galaxies. Not nebulae. Not, so far as any modern survey had ever recorded, any object at all. The coordinates were of blank patches of sky, distributed across what appeared to be a small ellipse of celestial longitude and latitude, in a region that no professional astronomer would, at any point in the last century, have had any particular reason to observe.

Her father had observed them for four years.

She had turned the pages back to the first entry. She had read the date. It was March 14, 1998. Her father would have been forty-eight. She had been five.

At the top of the first page, in his small careful hand, her father had written:

*Beginning the private observations. Coordinates as before. See separate file for method. To be shared with no one.*

Priya had sat in her father's office at six in the evening, on the fourth day of sorting his things, and had held the small black notebook in her lap.

She had thought: *there is a separate file.*

She had thought: *he has been observing something for twenty-seven years.*

She had turned the notebook back to the last entry. It was dated eleven years ago, three months before he had first been unable to work. The single word beside the last observation was:

*Closer.*

—

She did not open the other boxes that evening.

She sat in her father's office with the small black notebook in her lap, and she watched the light change in the small window that looked out onto the courtyard, and she thought.

She thought about her father.

She thought about the sort of man he had been. He had been, throughout her whole knowledge of him, a careful man. A precise man. A man who had, in his professional life, published exactly forty-one papers, all of them in respectable journals, none of them extraordinary, none of them, in the way of great scientific careers, foundational. He had been the sort of astronomer who had done his small competent work and had held his post at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics for thirty-four years and had retired with the small honors due a long and unremarkable career.

He had been, in his private life, similarly careful. He had been a devoted husband, in his way. He had been a distant but affectionate father. He had spent his evenings, throughout Priya's childhood, in this room, doing what she had understood at the time to be work.

He had been, apparently, doing something else.

He had been observing empty patches of sky, in a small ellipse across the Perseid-Andromedan boundary, for twenty-seven years. He had been doing this in secret. He had been keeping the observations in separate notebooks. He had, according to the note on the first page, kept a separate file describing the method — which meant that the observations were not merely a private hobby but a *program*, an organized long-term study, of something.

Of what?

She had, sitting in his office, been unable to answer.

She had been unable, at that moment, to consider whether the observations meant anything at all. They might have been the small private eccentricity of a competent astronomer who had, for reasons of his own, developed an interest in a particular section of empty sky. They might have been, in a mundane sense, nothing. She was aware of the possibility. She had, in her professional life, encountered enough eccentricities in enough older astronomers to know that they existed.

But her father had written, on the last page: *closer.*

Closer to what?

She had, at ten in the evening, gone to bed. She had lain in her old childhood bedroom, which her mother had preserved with the small careful conservation of an Indian mother preserving a daughter's childhood, and she had looked at the ceiling. She had thought about what she was going to do.

She had thought about telling her mother. She had considered this seriously. Her mother had been married to her father for forty-two years. Her mother might, she thought, know something about the observations. Her mother might, at least, have a right to know that they had existed.

She had considered, and had decided against.

She had understood, in the small dark of her childhood bedroom, that her father had left these notebooks to her. Not to her mother. Not to her brother. To her. He had, in the last years of his ability to do so, gathered together the whole of his working life into seventeen boxes, and had placed the black notebooks in a box labeled by year that would eventually come, in due order, to a daughter who was herself an astronomer, and who would, on opening the box, immediately recognize what she was looking at.

He had chosen her.

She had thought about this for a long time.

She had thought about the fact that he had never, in his life, told her about the observations. He had never, in the many long conversations they had had about astronomy over the years, mentioned them. He had, in the last years of his ability to speak, said many small halting things to her, and none of them had been about this.

He had said nothing. And then he had, in silence, given her everything.

She had understood, at three in the morning, lying in her childhood bedroom in her mother's house in Malleshwaram, what this meant.

It meant that he had wanted her to know only if she was willing to find out.

He had made her find the notebooks. He had made her open the box. He had made her, in the small ordinary work of sorting a dead father's papers, take the step of following the coordinates in a star atlas and discovering, on her own, that they were coordinates of nothing.

He had made her make the choice.

She had understood, at three in the morning, that she had already made it.

She had gotten up. She had gone back to the office. She had turned on the small green desk lamp. She had opened box eight.

chapters.title: The Method
chapters.body:
She found the method file on the sixth day.

It was not, as she had at first assumed, in one of the boxes. It was in the desk itself — in the shallow drawer above the kneehole, at the back, under a pile of old university receipts. Her father had put it where anyone cleaning out the drawer would find it, but only after they had found the notebooks first. It was, she thought when she found it, a small careful pedagogical arrangement.

The file was a manila folder, about a centimeter thick, tied with a soft cotton string. On the outside, in her father's small hand, was written:

*For P.*

She had held the folder for a moment.

She had, throughout her life, been called P by her father. It had been his private name for her. Her mother had called her Priya. Her brother had called her Priya. Her teachers had called her Priya. Only her father had called her P, in the small breath of his private affection, and only in the office, and only when he was in a good mood.

She had untied the string.

The folder contained about sixty pages of typed manuscript, in the specific slightly-off font of an old dot-matrix printer, with corrections and additions in her father's hand in several colors of ink over what she guessed was many years of revision. The first page, in the same hand as the label, read:

*Method for the observation of the Cassiopeia-Perseus objects. R. K. Ramesh. Begun March 1998. Revised continuously.*

She had sat down at the desk.

She had begun to read.

—

The first pages described, in the careful cautious prose of her father's public papers, the initial observation.

He had been, in early 1998, observing a field in Cassiopeia for a photometric variability study — one of the small standard programs that had produced perhaps a third of his published papers over the years — when he had noticed, on a single plate, a small point source that was not present on any of the other plates from the same night, or from the preceding weeks, or, so far as he had been able to determine over the following six months, from any earlier survey plate covering that field.

He had, initially, assumed the source was an artifact.

He had checked. He had run through the standard checks. He had ruled out cosmic ray hits. He had ruled out emulsion defects. He had ruled out satellite trails. He had ruled out reflection ghosts from bright stars elsewhere in the field. He had, over the course of that six months, ruled out every ordinary explanation for a single anomalous point source on a single plate.

He had, at the end of that six months, begun to observe the field systematically. Every clear night. For the next four years.

He had detected the source on approximately one night in fifteen.

He had determined, over the four years, that the source was not periodic — it did not come back at regular intervals — but that it was not random either. It appeared, disappeared, and reappeared in a pattern that his statistical tests could not entirely fit to any known variability class. It was not a Mira variable. It was not an eclipsing binary. It was not a supernova, or a nova, or a nova-like object. It was, in a phrase her father had used in the manuscript, *sui generis.*

Priya had, at the phrase, permitted herself a small smile. Her father had liked Latin. He had used it, in his public papers, more than was fashionable.

She had turned the page.

—

The next section described what her father had done in year five.

He had, having concluded that the source in Cassiopeia was not attributable to any known variable class, begun to look for additional sources of the same kind, elsewhere in the sky. He had done this on a hunch. He had had, he wrote, *no theoretical reason to expect further sources*, but had had *a certain intuition, difficult to articulate, that the Cassiopeia object was not solitary.*

He had spent the whole of years five and six searching.

He had found — she read, sitting at the desk — seventeen additional sources.

They were distributed, she saw as her father laid them out on a small hand-drawn chart included in the folder, across a specific region of sky. The region was not, as she had thought at first, an ellipse. It was a *shape*. It was an irregular closed figure that, when she looked at it on the chart, resembled — she blinked at it — resembled a splash. The kind of splash a drop of water made when it landed on a flat surface. A central concentration of sources, with several outliers arranged in a pattern of scattered radial fingers.

The central concentration was near the Perseid-Andromedan boundary.

The outlier fingers reached into Cepheus, into Cassiopeia, into a portion of Draco, into a small section of Camelopardalis.

The pattern was not, she thought as she looked at it, natural.

She had thought this instantly, without deliberation, on the strength of many years of looking at maps of stellar distributions. Stars did not distribute themselves in this pattern. Galaxies did not distribute themselves in this pattern. The pattern was — she had no other word for it — *deposited*. It was the shape of something that had, at some moment, been thrown at the sky from a single point, and had landed with a small radial dispersion.

Or the shape of something that had been *coming* from a single point, and had, in the moment her father was observing, arrived.

She had turned the page.

—

The next section described her father's analysis.

He had, over years seven through ten, subjected the eighteen sources to every form of astronomical analysis available to him. He had obtained spectra of six of them, over the course of a series of nights on the two-meter telescope at Kavalur which he had, using his considerable seniority, arranged to have without needing to write formal proposals. He had photometrically monitored all eighteen for a period of four years. He had checked their positions against every extant survey catalog, and had confirmed that none of them appeared in any survey that predated 1998, and that none of them had, at the moment he was observing, any counterpart at any wavelength other than the visible.

They had been visible only. Only in the visible. Only intermittently. And only, so far as he could determine, in the eighteen positions he had identified in Cassiopeia-Perseus.

He had, on year eleven, concluded — he wrote this in the manuscript with a small precise hedging that Priya recognized as the specific hedging of a scientist writing something he could not say directly — that the objects were not stars.

They were not, further, natural.

They were, he wrote, *objects of unknown provenance, arranged in a spatial distribution consistent with a single origin event or process.*

He had not, in the manuscript, speculated further.

He had not needed to.

Priya had read the section three times.

She had, on the third reading, understood that her father had believed the objects to be artificial.

He had believed that eighteen point sources of light, distributed across a hundred square degrees of sky in a splash pattern, appearing intermittently and only in the visible, and detectable so far as he had been able to determine only by himself, in the specific way he had been observing, were artificial.

He had not, of course, been able to publish this. He had not been able even to hint at it in any of his public work. Astronomers who claimed the discovery of artificial objects in the sky ended, in his profession, in one of two ways: laughed at, or removed. Her father had had no interest in either fate. He had, instead, made his forty-one careful competent public papers, and had gone home each evening to the small black notebooks, and had continued, for another sixteen years after the manuscript's date of composition, to observe.

Priya had turned to the last section of the manuscript.

—

The last section had a heading in her father's hand, added later:

*Provisional interpretation.*

It was three pages long.

It was written, unlike the rest of the manuscript, in a first person. In the earlier sections her father had used the passive voice of scientific prose — *observations were made*, *the data were reduced*, *conclusions can be drawn*. In this section he had, apparently, permitted himself the *I*.

He had written:

*I have, over the last eighteen years, watched these objects. I have watched them without hope of publication, without expectation of vindication, and without, in the end, any need for either. I have watched them because they are there. I have watched them because I am, so far as I can determine, the only person in the world who has seen them. This has not always been a comfortable position. It is, however, mine.*

*I do not know what the objects are. I have not been able to determine, from their spectra, whether they are near or far. If they are near — within, say, a hundred light-years — they would be, at their observed brightness, small: perhaps the size of small satellites, perhaps smaller. If they are far — thousands of light-years, or more — they would be enormous. I have not been able to distinguish the two cases from my observations. There is no parallax detectable at my instruments' resolution, which tells me only that they are not extremely near.*

*I have not been able to determine, from their behavior, whether they are moving. Their positions on the sky have not changed measurably in eighteen years. If they are moving toward us or away from us, this movement is not, at my instruments' resolution, detectable.*

*I have, however, become steadily more convinced, without being able to justify this conviction from the observations, that they are moving toward us.*

Priya had, at this sentence, put the manuscript down.

She had sat at the desk for a long moment.

She had picked it up.

She had continued reading:

*I make this statement here, in this document that no one will read except my daughter, because I do not wish to record it anywhere else. It is not scientific. It is not defensible. It is, however, what I believe. I believe that the objects are approaching. I believe that they have been approaching, at whatever rate, for the whole of the eighteen years I have been observing them, and probably for far longer. I believe that they were, at some earlier point, farther away, and that we could not have seen them then; and that they are, at the moment of my writing, close enough to be intermittently visible in an eight-inch amateur refractor from the balcony of a house in Malleshwaram; and that they will, at some point that I cannot predict but that I do not think is far off in cosmological time, be closer still.*

*I do not know what will happen when they arrive.*

*I do not think anyone will know until it happens.*

Priya had, at this last sentence, permitted herself, for the first time since she had opened box seven, a small quiet fear.

She had sat with the fear.

She had sat with it for perhaps an hour, at the desk in her father's office, in the small green light of the desk lamp. She had let it move through her. She had not fought it.

When it had passed, or had at least receded to some manageable level, she had turned to the last page of the manuscript.

The last page had a single paragraph.

It read:

*P. I have left you the notebooks and this file because you are the only person in my life who might, if you choose, continue the observations. I do not ask you to. I do not, in fact, think you should. I have, over the last eighteen years, given a great deal of my life to this project, and I am not certain, in retrospect, that the project has given me anything commensurate. It has been lonely. It has been, at times, unbalancing. It has been very much a private matter, and there are things, I think, which perhaps ought to remain private.*

*You may, if you wish, destroy this file. You may destroy the notebooks. You may, having read this manuscript, forget the coordinates and never look at that region of sky again. This would, I think, be a reasonable choice.*

*You may also, if you wish, continue. The instructions for the observations are in the notebooks. The coordinates are there. The methods are here. If you continue, I ask only that you keep the observations private, as I have done. I have not published because I have not wished to be laughed at, and because I have not wished to see this taken up by others who would treat it badly. If you continue, you will have to make the same choices.*

*Whatever you choose, know that I have loved you. I have loved you, and I have watched you become, in the years I have watched, a better astronomer than I ever was. I am, at the end, glad I have had you to leave this to. Whether or not you take it, it is now yours.*

*With love,*

*Your father.*

The letter was signed, in his careful hand:

*R. K. Ramesh, 12 March 2014.*

He had written the letter, she saw, eleven years before he had died. He had been sixty-four. He had, at the time of writing, still been able to observe. He had gone on observing for another three years. He had gone on packing the boxes for another four after that.

He had prepared this letter — she understood, sitting at his desk in the green lamplight — knowing that eleven years might pass before she read it.

She sat with the letter for a long time.

At the end of that long time she stood up. She switched off the desk lamp. She left the office. She went to the small balcony of the house, which faced east, and looked, from the eastern edge of Malleshwaram, over the neighboring rooftops toward the dawn.

The stars were still out. The eastern sky was, at that hour, at the deep clear blue of the last half hour before sunrise. Cassiopeia was low, and just barely visible.

She looked at it.

She thought: *I will decide tomorrow.*

She thought this the way one thinks something one already knows one is not going to do.

She had already decided.

chapters.title: The Watch
chapters.body:
She continued.

She continued in Cambridge. She had, on returning from Bangalore, arranged for her mother to ship the seventeen boxes to her — she had done this quietly, without fanfare, telling her mother she wished to catalog her father's papers over the following year — and had received them in her small flat in West Cambridge in early winter. She had unpacked the black notebooks and the method file, and had put the other fifty or so notebooks of her father's public work in the spare room, and had, over the following six months, done what her father had done: she had gone into the small local observation with her borrowed equipment on every clear night, and had checked the eighteen positions.

She had detected sources on approximately one night in fifteen.

The rate had not changed since her father's last observations. But the sources — she had understood over the course of the six months — were closer.

They were, more precisely, *brighter.* The apparent magnitudes she was measuring were, at each of the eighteen positions, brighter by about a fifth of a magnitude than the values her father had recorded in his last year of observations. She had verified this against several of her father's late measurements. She had verified it against the specific calibration stars her father had used and had, herself, continued to use.

The sources were brightening.

If they were brightening because they were moving toward us — which was, she believed, the simplest explanation, though not the only one — then they had, in the eleven years since her father had last measured them, closed a fraction of their distance.

She could not, from the brightening alone, determine what fraction. She had, in a small notebook of her own — a plain green Moleskine that she had bought at the university bookshop, because she had not been able to bring herself to use one of her father's remaining unfilled black notebooks — computed the fractional change in flux and had produced a range of possible distance changes depending on assumed geometry. The range was wide. The lower bound was small. The upper bound was substantial.

She had not, when computing the upper bound, permitted herself to consider what a substantial closing implied.

She had continued observing.

—

She had, on the ninth month of her observations, added a new position.

She had done this without justification. She had, one night in July, been observing the innermost of the original eighteen positions — the central concentration of the splash pattern, near the boundary of Perseus and Andromeda — and had, without particular reason, decided to observe a slightly offset position, three arcminutes to the east of the central concentration. She had done this in the way an experienced observer sometimes did an unplanned pointing, on instinct.

She had detected a source at the offset position.

The source was faint. It was at the very edge of what her small telescope could resolve at that limiting magnitude, on that night, in the specific seeing conditions. But it was, she was confident, real. She had run through the checks. She had ruled out cosmic ray hits. She had checked for reflection ghosts. She had verified against the standard star catalogs.

It was a new source. It was not among the eighteen her father had identified. It was, three arcminutes east of the central concentration, in a location he had never, so far as his manuscript indicated, looked.

She had, over the following month, tested seven more positions along a small circular offset from the central concentration.

She had found four more sources.

She had understood, at the end of that month, that her father had catalogued only what he had, by pure attention and hard patience, been able to find. She had understood that the *actual* distribution of the sources was probably far denser than his eighteen. She had understood that the splash pattern was not, as she had at first believed, a scattered array of eighteen points, but a *field* — a densely populated region of many hundreds, perhaps thousands, of point sources, of which her father had detected only the brightest, and of which she was now detecting fainter members as her observations continued.

The field was, so far as she could tell from the boundary sources, larger than the region her father had mapped.

It was extending itself.

It was, in fact, spreading — in the manner of a splash still expanding on the surface of a pond, though in the sky, and slowly.

She had sat with this understanding for some time.

She had understood, at the same time, that whatever she was observing was not, could not be, a splash *in* the sky. The sky did not receive splashes. The distances involved were too great for anything to have propagated across them in a way that would produce the appearance of a still-expanding pattern in her lifetime, or in her father's lifetime, or in any combined lifetime she could reasonably consider.

What she was observing was, therefore, either much closer than her father had assumed, or was expanding at a rate that suggested something other than physical motion.

Or was doing both.

She had not, in the small green Moleskine, written this last sentence down. She had not permitted herself.

—

By the eighteenth month of her observations she had catalogued three hundred and seven sources.

She had, by then, developed a small private routine. She observed on every clear night, from the small pier telescope she had negotiated access to at the Institute — a five-inch that no one else used — and she recorded her measurements in the Moleskine and cross-referenced them against her father's manuscript file and against her growing catalog of new sources. She had, during the days, continued her professional work — she had, over the course of that eighteen months, published two papers and given three conference talks, all on subjects that had nothing to do with the sources — and had, by every ordinary measure, remained a functional postdoctoral researcher of thirty-four years of age.

She had also, over the course of that eighteen months, gradually stopped seeing other people.

She had done this without noticing at first. She had, on a Tuesday in March, realized that she had not had dinner with anyone other than her supervisor in seven weeks. She had, on a Saturday in May, realized that she had not been to a party or a pub or a dinner since Christmas. She had, on a Wednesday in July, realized that her closest friend at the Institute — a South African postdoc named Nadine, whom she had been meeting for coffee every Wednesday for two years — had, in the last three months, stopped inviting her. Nadine had, gradually and without ceremony, given up on her.

Priya had considered this. She had considered writing to Nadine to apologize. She had considered arranging to see her.

She had not done so.

She had understood, sitting at her desk on that Wednesday in July, that she had chosen the observations over the friendship without ever, at any moment, making the choice. It had happened by accumulation. Every Wednesday evening for four months, when Nadine would ordinarily have suggested coffee, Priya had, without noticing, been unavailable — because it was clear, or because she was reducing data from the previous night, or because she was, quite simply, tired from having been up until four in the morning at the small pier telescope.

She had chosen the sources.

She had understood, further, that she was going to go on choosing them. She was going to spend the next thirty or forty or fifty years — however many years the universe granted her — observing the sources, and she was going to become, in that time, the sort of astronomer her father had been: technically competent, publicly modest, privately consumed. She was going to spend her evenings in front of her telescope. She was going to keep her small precise Moleskine. She was going to catalog the sources as they multiplied, and she was going to watch them, over the course of decades, grow brighter, and expand, and — at whatever rate they were coming — come.

She had, that Wednesday evening, sat at her desk for a long time.

She had, at last, opened the small green Moleskine.

She had turned to a blank page at the back.

She had written, in her small quick hand:

*I have understood tonight what my father understood. I have understood why he did not tell my mother. Why he did not tell me. Why he wrote the manuscript, and packed the boxes, and left them for me to find only after he was dead. He was, in the end, not doing this for science. He was doing it because it was his. He had, at some point in the first years of the observations, been chosen — or had chosen himself, which is I suppose the same thing — and had given the rest of his life to the watching. He had accepted a small private priesthood. He had done this quietly and had told no one. He had, in the end, when he could no longer perform the observations himself, passed the priesthood to me.*

*I have accepted it.*

*I have accepted it, I think, because he asked. I have accepted it also because the sources have, in eighteen months, brightened by an average of eleven percent, which suggests they are getting closer, and because it is possible — I have to admit, sitting here, that it is possible — that they will arrive in my lifetime, or in the lifetime of my brother's children, or in the lifetime of anyone alive on Earth today. If they arrive, someone should have been watching.*

*I am the person who has been watching.*

*I am not sure this makes any difference. I am not sure it will make any difference when they arrive, if they arrive, what any single astronomer on Earth has been doing with a small telescope in a small city. But I know that my father would have wanted someone to have been watching, and I am, so far as I can tell, the person who has agreed.*

*I write this so that if — at some point in the coming years or decades — someone opens my papers as I opened his, they will find this and know.*

*Someone was watching.*

*It was me.*

She had closed the Moleskine.

She had turned off the desk lamp.

She had gone to the window of her small West Cambridge flat, and had looked, up over the roof of the next-door house, at the eastern sky.

Cassiopeia was rising.

She had watched it for a moment.

Then she had put on her coat, and had taken her key from the small dish by the door, and had gone out into the cold July night to walk the two miles to the Institute's pier telescope. There was, by her calculation, another six hours of dark, and the seeing was, at that hour, good, and there was in Perseus a new sector she had not yet fully mapped.

She had time. She had, if the sources were coming at the rate she thought they were, some decades still. She meant to use them.

She had walked into the night.

—

The observations continued for forty-one more years.

Priya Ramesh maintained them faithfully from the age of thirty-four until her death, at seventy-eight, of the same neurological condition that had taken her father, in a hospice in Grantchester in the spring of a wet cold year. She had, in that time, catalogued more than sixteen thousand sources, and had watched the splash pattern expand across nearly a quarter of the northern sky, and had watched the individual sources brighten by an average factor of five since her first observations. She had not, at any point, published a word about any of it.

Her boxes — twenty-two of them, blue rather than her father's brown, containing forty-one years of Moleskine notebooks and calibration data and her own long manuscript file titled *For whoever* — were, in her will, left to a young astronomer at the Institute whom she had, quietly, over the last decade of her life, been mentoring.

The young astronomer, whose name was Elena, opened the first box on a Tuesday in November.

The observations continued.

They continue still, so far as anyone knows. In a small pier telescope in Cambridge, or in a small refractor on a balcony in Malleshwaram, or in some other quiet place, someone is watching. The sources are, at whatever rate they are coming, coming.

There will always, so long as anyone is left to keep the watch, be someone.
